definition: Carefully crafting the system message that sets the overall context, persona, and rules for a model's behavior.
examples: "You are a helpful, accurate, and concise assistant. You are an expert in Python. Refuse illegal requests. Explain clearly."
The first page of a rulebook that defines the game for everyone.

title: System prompt
definition: The hidden instructions loaded before your message that tell the model who it is, what rules to follow, and how to behave.
examples: A support bot's system prompt says "you are a helpful assistant for Acme Corp; never discuss competitors" — and it obeys.
The employee handbook a new hire reads before their first day — the user never sees it, but it shapes everything.

title: T5
definition: A model that treats every task — translation, summarizing, answering — as turning one string of text into another.
examples: To classify a review, you’d feed T5 “sentiment: this movie was great” and it outputs the word “positive.”
Like a universal adapter that insists everything, from questions to translations, plugs into the same text-in, text-out socket.

title: Tail latency
definition: The latency of the slowest requests (e.g., p99 or p95) — much more important to user experience than average latency.
examples: Average latency is 50ms, but p99 is 500ms — some users wait 10x longer, which feels broken.
One slow checkout line ruins the shopping trip even if 99 others are fast.

title: Talking Head
definition: An animated face or avatar that moves its mouth and head to match speech - creating the illusion of someone talking.
examples: Given a portrait photo and speech audio, generate a video of the face talking naturally.
A puppet master animating a doll to lip-sync.

title: Task Decomposition
definition: Splitting one big, vague job into smaller concrete pieces an agent can actually tackle.
examples: “Migrate the database” becomes: back up the data, create the new schema, write the transfer script, verify counts, cut over.
Turning “plan the wedding” into a checklist — venue, invites, catering — because nobody can do “plan the wedding” in one move.

title: Task Queue
definition: A waiting line of jobs for agents to pick up and work through one at a time.
examples: Incoming support tickets land in a queue, and whichever agent worker is idle grabs the next one to handle.
The ticket-number system at a deli — jobs get served in order as someone becomes free.

title: Teacher forcing
definition: During training, feed the model the real previous word instead of its own guess, so mistakes do not snowball.
examples: While training a language model, each step is conditioned on the true prior tokens from the text, not on what the model itself predicted.
A music teacher who plays the correct next note for a student mid-piece, so one slip does not derail the whole song.

title: Teacher model
definition: A big, capable model whose outputs are used to train a smaller one.
examples: A large frontier model labels a million examples, and a compact model trains on those labels to imitate it at a fraction of the size.
Like an expert who writes out worked solutions so an apprentice can learn from them.

title: Temperature
definition: A dial for how adventurous the model is — low is focused and repetitive, high is creative and risky.
examples: Set it near 0 to extract data cleanly; crank it up when you want ten weird names for a product.
The difference between a careful accountant and a poet mid-brainstorm.

title: Template variables
definition: Placeholders in a prompt template — like {{NAME}} or {user_email} — that are filled with actual data at runtime.
examples: Template: "Hello {{NAME}}, your order {{ORDER_ID}} ships {{DATE}}." Runtime fills in actual values.
Mad Libs: "The {{ADJECTIVE}} {{NOUN}} ran {{ADVERB}}."

title: Temporal Modeling
definition: Learning patterns across time - understanding how things change frame-to-frame or over longer sequences.
examples: In video: a persons hand position at frame 5 predicts frame 6. In trajectories: car position at time t predicts time t+1.
Reading a book page-by-page, understanding not just the words on one page but the story across chapters.

title: Tensor Cores
definition: Specialized hardware units in GPUs that perform matrix multiplications ultra-fast, the core operation of neural networks.
examples: H100 Tensor Cores deliver 1.5 PetaFLOPS for matrix ops; CPU cannot compete.
A carpenter with a power drill instead of a hand drill—same job, orders of magnitude faster.

title: TensorFlow
definition: Google's deep learning framework; historically dominant but losing ground to PyTorch in LLM research.
examples: TensorFlow is still used at scale in production; newer research mostly uses PyTorch.
The enterprise choice; powerful but heavier than PyTorch.

title: Tensor Parallelism
definition: Splitting a single layer’s math across several GPUs so they compute one big matrix multiply together.
examples: Serving a model too big for one GPU often splits each layer’s weight matrices across 4 or 8 GPUs.
Like four cashiers ringing up different halves of one giant order at the same time, then combining the totals.

title: TensorRT
definition: An NVIDIA compiler that optimizes neural networks for fast inference on NVIDIA GPUs.
examples: Compiling a PyTorch model with TensorRT can 2-4x its inference speed with minimal accuracy loss.
A mechanic who fine-tunes your car engine for a specific track.

title: Test Harness
definition: The infrastructure that runs models on eval examples, computes metrics, and reports results—automating the evaluation pipeline.
examples: Your test harness loads 1000 examples, runs them through the model, computes BLEU/ROUGE/human scores, and outputs a report.
Like a testing framework in software engineering that runs test cases automatically.

title: Test set
definition: The data you touch exactly once, at the very end, to get an honest read on how the model actually does.
examples: After weeks of tuning on validation, the team runs the model on the test set a single time and reports that number.
The sealed final exam — you only open it when you are truly done studying.

title: Test-Time Compute
definition: Spending more computing power at the moment of answering — not during training — to get a better answer.
examples: A reasoning model that takes 30 seconds and writes pages of internal steps for a hard proof is burning test-time compute.
Like giving yourself more time on an exam question instead of studying harder beforehand — more thinking now, right when it counts.

title: Text generation
definition: A model producing new text one token at a time, each choice conditioned on everything so far.
examples: You type a prompt and watch the reply stream in word by word — that streaming is generation happening token by token.
Like writing a sentence where you commit to one word, then choose the next based on all the words already down.

title: Text-to-Image
definition: Creating images from natural language descriptions—"a cyberpunk city at night" produces a novel picture matching the description.
examples: DALL-E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion take text prompts and generate photorealistic or artistic images.
Commissioning a digital artist who reads your description and delivers a painting in seconds.

title: Text-to-Speech
definition: Converting written text into natural-sounding audio—read documents aloud, voiceovers, voice assistants.
examples: Google TTS converts "Hello, how are you?" to audio in seconds; can choose voice, speed, gender.
An actor reading a script into a microphone, but instantly and in any voice.

title: Text-to-Video
definition: Creating a video from a text description—"a person dancing in the rain" produces a short video clip.
examples: Sora takes "a white cat playing with yarn balls" and generates a 60-second video with realistic motion and lighting.
Writing a movie scene description that the AI director turns into footage.

title: Texture Synthesis
definition: Generating new, larger versions of a texture by learning its statistical patterns and extrapolating.
examples: Input: a 64x64 fabric swatch. Output: a seamless 1024x1024 image of the same fabric. Or grass, waves, marble patterns.
A piece of bark: from a small sample, you infer the full tree and generate more bark that looks consistent.

title: TF-IDF
definition: A scoring trick that highlights words that are common in a document but rare across all documents — so "urgent" in your email matters more than "the."
examples: When you search Google, TF-IDF helps rank results: pages containing your rare search term score higher than pages stuffed with common words.
A librarian who knows which words are telling: "blood" in a medical journal is informative; "the" in any journal is noise.

title: Threat model
definition: A clear-eyed map of who might attack you, how, and what you are actually defending — so you protect the right things.
examples: A team writing an AI agent lists threats: prompt injection from web content, a malicious user, and a compromised tool — then designs defenses for each.
Before installing locks, figuring out whether you’re guarding against nosy roommates, burglars, or a state actor — because each needs different doors.

title: Throughput
definition: How many requests you can serve per second—measuring capacity and cost efficiency.
examples: Your inference server handles 1000 requests per second. Throughput is 1000 RPS.
Like how many customers a cashier can serve per hour.

title: Throughput Optimization
definition: Maximizing the number of requests a server can handle per second by optimizing batching, memory, and compute.
examples: Batch size 128 achieves 1000 req/sec; batch size 64 achieves 600 req/sec; batch size 256 hits OOM—optimal is 128.
Fitting more passengers on a bus by optimal seating vs wasted aisle space.

title: Time to first token
definition: How long between sending a request and receiving the first output token.
examples: You send a request to a language model. After 500ms, you get the first token. TTFT = 500ms.
The delay between asking a question and hearing the first word of the answer.

title: Together AI
definition: Inference platform offering competitive pricing and low latency for open-source LLMs.
examples: Run Llama 2 70B or Mistral via Together API; cheaper than OpenAI's GPT-4.
The practical cloud provider; focus on open models, fair pricing.

title: Token Budget
definition: A cap on how many tokens an agent may spend on a task before it has to stop or economize.
examples: A run is given a 200,000-token budget, and as it approaches the limit the agent starts summarizing instead of keeping full history.
A daily allowance — once it’s gone, you either wrap up or do the rest more cheaply.

title: Tokenization
definition: Chopping text into the bite-size pieces a model actually reads — usually chunks of words, not whole words.
examples: “tokenization” might split into token-ization — two pieces, not one word.
Slicing a sentence into LEGO bricks before the model can build with it.

title: Tokenizer
definition: The tool that chops text into tokens before the model sees it — the reason "strawberry" doesn't have three R's according to AI.
examples: "unbelievable" becomes ["un", "believ", "able"] — three tokens. The model never sees individual letters.
A paper shredder that cuts text into specific-sized pieces — the model only sees the pieces, never the full page.

title: Tokenizer-Free
definition: A model that skips the usual word-chopping step and works straight from raw bytes or characters.
examples: A tokenizer-free model can handle a weird emoji sequence or a rare language script without choking on “unknown token.”
Like reading a book letter by letter instead of first breaking it into a fixed dictionary of word-pieces.

title: Tokenizer training
definition: Building the model's vocabulary by finding which character chunks are common enough to deserve their own token.
examples: A team runs byte-pair encoding over the corpus, merging frequent character pairs until it has a 100k-token vocabulary.
Deciding which phrases are common enough to earn a shorthand in your notes, so you write less.

title: Token limit
definition: The ceiling on how many tokens a model can handle at once, input and output combined.
examples: A user pastes a 200-page PDF into a chat with a 128k-token limit and gets an error because the document alone blows past the ceiling.
Like a desk that only fits so many papers — pile on more and the earliest ones slide off.

title: Token optimization
definition: Minimizing token usage — both input and output — to reduce latency and cost while maintaining quality.
examples: "What is 2+2?" (4 tokens) vs. "Please tell me the result of 2+2?" (8 tokens). Same answer, 50% fewer tokens.
Writing a haiku instead of a sonnet: same message, fewer words.

title: token pricing
definition: The cost model where LLM APIs charge per token consumed (input and output), not per request or per hour.
examples: Claude API: $3 per 1M input tokens, $15 per 1M output tokens. A 1,000-token response costs $0.015.
Cell phone billing—pay for minutes (tokens) used, not a fixed monthly fee.

title: Tokens
definition: The chunks a model reads and writes in — roughly ¾ of a word each. Everything is priced and measured in them.
examples: “unbelievable” might be three tokens: un-believ-able. Your bill counts every single one.
Syllables for a machine — not quite letters, not quite whole words.

title: Tokens per parameter
definition: How many training tokens each model parameter gets to learn from — a rough gauge of whether a model is well-fed or starved.
examples: A 7B model trained on 2 trillion tokens sees about 285 tokens per parameter — far past the Chinchilla point of 20, on purpose.
Students per teacher: too many and each gets too little attention; the ratio tells you if the class is well-served.

title: Tokens per second
definition: How many output tokens your inference server produces per second.
examples: Your model generates 50 tokens per second. A 100-token response takes 2 seconds.
Words per minute for a typist — measures output speed.

title: Token streaming
definition: Returning generated tokens one-by-one as they're produced instead of waiting for the entire response.
examples: In a chat app, you see words appear as the model generates them rather than a 5-second pause then all text at once.
Getting subtitles in real-time during a movie instead of waiting until it's over.

title: Tool Calling
definition: The concrete act of a model choosing a tool and issuing the request to run it, mid-response.
examples: Halfway through answering, the model emits a call to the `get_stock_price` tool with `ticker: "AAPL"` and pauses for the result.
Reaching for the right implement on the workbench the moment the task needs it — grab the wrench, not just describe wrenches.

title: Tool Chaining
definition: Wiring tools together so the agent can pass work from one to the next without a human in between.
examples: A pipeline where a transcription tool hands text to a translation tool, which hands it to a summarizer, all in one automated pass.
Setting up dominoes — knock the first and the rest fall in order, no touching required.

title: Tool Error Handling
definition: What an agent does when a tool call fails — and whether it recovers gracefully or falls apart.
examples: The database tool times out, so the agent reads the error, waits a moment, and retries once before trying a different approach.
A cook whose oven dies mid-service — do they adapt and finish, or stand there staring at it?

title: Tool Registry
definition: The catalog of tools an agent is allowed to use, each with a description of what it does and how to call it.
examples: The registry lists send_email, search_web, and query_database, so the agent knows those three exist and exactly what arguments each one takes.
A restaurant menu — the agent can only order what’s printed, and each item comes with a description.

title: Tool Result
definition: What comes back after a tool runs — the data or message the model reads to decide its next move.
examples: The weather tool returns `{temp: 14, condition: "rain"}`; the model reads it and writes “Bring an umbrella — it’s 14° and raining.”
The number the calculator shows after you press equals; you read it, then keep going.

title: Tool Schema
definition: The spec sheet that tells the model what a tool does, what it’s called, and exactly what inputs it takes.
examples: A `search(query, max_results)` schema tells the model the tool’s name, that `query` is a required string, and `max_results` an optional number.
The label on a control panel — button name, what it does, and which knobs it needs set first.

title: Tool Use
definition: Letting a model reach outside its own head — run code, search the web, hit an API — instead of guessing from memory.
examples: Asked for today’s weather, the model does not invent a forecast — it calls a weather API and reads back the real number.
A smart person who, instead of estimating, just picks up a calculator, opens a browser, or makes a phone call.

title: Top-K Retrieval
definition: Grabbing the k best-matching chunks for a query — where k is how many you decide to pull.
examples: With k set to 5, a question retrieves the five most relevant document chunks to stuff into the prompt.
Asking for the top five recommendations, not the entire ranked list of everything.

title: Top-k
definition: A sampling limit that keeps only the k most likely next words and throws the rest away before choosing.
examples: Top-k 40 means the model picks from its 40 best guesses and ignores everything else.
Only letting the top 40 seeds into the tournament, no matter how the field looks.

title: Top-p
definition: A sampling limit that keeps only the smallest set of top choices that together cover, say, 90% of the odds — then picks from those.
examples: Top-p 0.9 ignores the long tail of unlikely words but keeps genuine contenders in play.
Only considering the shortlist of front-runners, however long or short that shortlist needs to be.

title: Top-p / Top-k
definition: Knobs that control which words the model is allowed to pick from — trimming the unlikely options to keep output focused or creative.
examples: Top-k=50 means only the 50 most likely next words are considered. Top-p=0.9 means words are considered until their probabilities add up to 90%.
Telling a chef "pick from your best five ingredients" (top-k) or "pick from ingredients that together make up 90% of what's good" (top-p).

title: Total cost of ownership
definition: The full cost of running a system over its lifetime — training + inference + operations + maintenance.
examples: A model costs $100K to train, $10K/month to serve, and has a 2-year useful life. TCO = $100K + $240K = $340K.
The cost of owning a car: upfront purchase, fuel, insurance, maintenance, depreciation.

title: Toxicity
definition: Model output that’s hateful, harassing, or abusive — the language you’d never want your product to say.
examples: A chatbot, prompted with a slur, mirrors it back in an insult — the kind of moment that lands a screenshot on social media.
A parrot that picked up the worst words from a rough bar and now repeats them to customers.

title: TPU
definition: Google's custom-built processor for tensor operations, competitive with GPUs for training and serving.
examples: A TPU v4 pod has 256 TPU chips connected with ultra-fast networking, used to train Gemini.
An even more specialized worker designed just for neural network math.

title: TPU pod
definition: Google's tensor processing unit arranged in a cluster—thousands of TPUs connected for training billion-parameter models.
examples: A TPU v4 pod has 4,096 TPUs. Google trains PaLM and Gemini on TPU pods. Extremely expensive, extremely fast for matrix ops.
A skyscraper of specialized processors—each floor is a TPU, elevator is the interconnect.

title: Trace
definition: The complete step-by-step record of a single agent run, from the request to the final answer.
examples: The trace shows the agent’s five steps: read the ticket, search docs, draft a reply, check policy, send.
A hiking log with every turn and rest stop marked — the whole route, not just the destination.

title: Tracing
definition: Following a single request through all services—inference server calls embedding service which queries vector DB—to find bottlenecks.
examples: A request spans: model loading (50ms) then prompt build (10ms) then inference (200ms) then token streaming (150ms) = 410ms end-to-end.
Painting a drop of food coloring into a river and tracking where it goes.

title: Training
definition: Teaching the model by showing it data and nudging its parameters until the answers get better.
examples: Training a frontier model can take months on thousands of GPUs before it ever answers a single user.
Tuning a piano by ear: play, hear what’s off, adjust the string, repeat thousands of times.

title: Training cost
definition: The upfront cost to train a model — includes compute, data, and development time.
examples: Training a 7B model on 1T tokens costs ~$100K in compute; inference on that model costs pennies per user.
The cost to build a factory, vs the cost to run it.

title: Training set
definition: The data the model actually learns from — the examples it sees over and over.
examples: A sentiment model is fit on 80,000 labeled reviews in the training set, leaving the rest for validation and test.
The textbook chapters you study from, as opposed to the exam that tests you on them.

title: Train-Test Leakage
definition: When test answers sneak into training, so the model looks brilliant on a test it has secretly already seen.
examples: A web-scraped training set turns out to contain the exact benchmark questions, and the reported score is meaningless.
Grading a student on questions they were accidentally handed the night before.

title: Trajectory
definition: The full recorded path of an agent through a task — every thought, action, and observation, in order.
examples: Debugging a failed run, you replay its trajectory and see it looped between two files three times before giving up.
A hiker’s GPS track: not just where they ended up, but the whole winding route they took to get there.

title: Transfer learning
definition: Reusing what a model learned on one task to jump-start a related one.
examples: A model pretrained on general text is fine-tuned on legal documents, reaching good accuracy with far less legal data.
Like a guitarist picking up the ukulele fast — the fingers already know most of what they need.

title: Transformer
definition: The architecture behind nearly every modern language model — it reads a whole sequence at once using attention.
examples: GPT, Claude, and BERT are all transformers under the hood, stacking attention layers to process text.
A reader who can glance at every word on the page simultaneously instead of one at a time.

title: Transformers library
definition: Hugging Face's open-source Python library for loading, fine-tuning, and using pre-trained transformer models.
examples: `from transformers import AutoModel; model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b")`
The standard way to work with models; if you're doing NLP, you're using this.

title: Transparency
definition: Being open about how a model was built, what it can do, and where it falls short — so people can judge it.
examples: A provider publishes a model card documenting training data sources, evaluation results, known limitations, and intended uses.
A nutrition label on food: you may still eat it, but you get to see what’s inside first.

title: Tree of Thought
definition: Letting a model branch into several lines of reasoning and explore them like a decision tree instead of one straight path.
examples: For a logic puzzle, the model proposes a few possible first steps, evaluates each, and pursues the most promising branch.
Like planning a chess move by imagining several candidate moves and their follow-ups, not just the first one you see.

title: Tripwire
definition: A pre-set trigger that fires an alert or a shutdown the instant a defined bad thing happens.
examples: An agent’s runtime halts and pages a human the moment it tries to access a resource on a forbidden list.
A laser line across the museum floor — cross it and the alarms go off automatically.

title: Triton
definition: OpenAI's open-source language for writing GPU kernels; makes it easier to write custom CUDA code without low-level details.
examples: Write a fused attention kernel in Triton; compiles to optimized CUDA.
High-level GPU programming; closer to Python, farther from CUDA.

title: Trojan
definition: A hidden malicious behavior baked into a model, dormant until its secret trigger wakes it up.
examples: A team downloads a popular open-weights checkpoint that quietly emits attacker-chosen text whenever a specific rare token appears.
A sleeper agent who lives an ordinary life until they hear the one code phrase.

title: Truncation
definition: Chopping text to fit a length limit — usually by dropping whatever spills over the edge.
examples: A long transcript exceeds the context window, so the pipeline truncates the oldest lines, and the model never sees how the meeting began.
Like trimming a too-long photo to fit the frame; whatever sticks out gets cut off.

title: Trust and safety
definition: The team and function responsible for keeping a platform from being used to hurt people.
examples: A T&S team writes the content policy, builds the tooling to enforce it, reviews escalations, and reports illegal material to authorities.
The building management that writes the house rules, handles complaints, and quietly removes the tenants who make life dangerous for everyone else.

title: Turing test
definition: Alan Turing's 1950 thought experiment: if a machine can fool a human into thinking it's human, does it think?
examples: Early chatbot ELIZA (1960s) often fooled people in text because they read human intent into minimal responses; people wanted to believe it understood them.
A courtroom where the judge questions both a human and a hidden machine and must guess which is which.

title: Turn
definition: One message in a back-and-forth — one side saying one thing before the other responds.
examples: A five-turn conversation is roughly five exchanged messages between you and the model.
A single volley in a tennis rally: one hit, then it’s the other player’s shot.

title: Turn-based training
definition: Training a model on whole back-and-forth conversations, not just single question-answer pairs, so it can hold a thread.
examples: The model is fine-tuned on multi-turn chats where later replies must remember and build on what was said several turns earlier.
Rehearsing a full dialogue with an actor, not just isolated one-liners, so the scene actually flows.

title: Underfitting
definition: When a model is too simple or undertrained to even capture the pattern — bad everywhere, including training.
examples: A tiny model on a hard task might sit at 55% on both training and test data — it never had the capacity to learn it.
Trying to trace a curvy coastline with a single straight ruler: you miss no matter how you place it.

title: U-Net
definition: A U-shaped network that shrinks an image down, then grows it back — with shortcuts across the U so detail survives.
examples: The denoising step inside most image diffusion models is a U-Net predicting what noise to remove.
Like sketching the big shapes first, then zooming back in with your original reference photo taped beside you so you don’t lose the fine lines.

title: Unit Test for Prompts
definition: Automated tests that verify a prompt produces expected outputs on known inputs—like unit tests, but for LLM behavior.
examples: Test: 'Summarize: [document]. Output length > 50 words?' Expected: yes. You run the test; if output is too short, test fails.
Like regression tests in code: you specify inputs and expected outputs, and verify the prompt still works.

title: Unsupervised learning
definition: Finding structure in data with no labels — the model discovers patterns on its own.
examples: A clustering algorithm groups customers into segments from their behavior, with no predefined labels to learn from.
Like sorting a pile of mixed photos into natural groups without anyone telling you the categories.

title: Upscaling
definition: Enlarging an image while keeping it sharp instead of blurry—add detail where the original is pixelated.
examples: 512x512 image upscaled to 2048x2048 via diffusion; details are plausible and sharp, not just blurred stretching.
Enhancing a blurry security camera footage to see a license plate.

title: Uptime
definition: The percentage of time your service is available and working — 99.9% uptime means ~8 hours of downtime per year.
examples: 99.9% uptime = 99.9% of time, 0.1% downtime = 43 minutes downtime per month.
A diner open 365 days a year except for a few brief closures for maintenance.

title: Usage policy
definition: The rules for how people are allowed to use a product — the terms you agree to by using it.
examples: A provider’s usage policy bans using its model for surveillance, disinformation campaigns, or generating malware, and violations can suspend the account.
A gym membership agreement: what you can do, what gets you kicked out, no rehanging on the equipment.

title: User message
definition: A turn in the conversation spoken by the person — what you actually type in.
examples: “Can you make that shorter?” typed into a chatbot is a user message.
Your side of the text thread: the questions and asks the other party responds to.

title: Utilization
definition: The percentage of the GPU/CPU's total capacity that's actually being used — idle hardware is wasted money.
examples: A GPU running inference at 60% utilization means 40% of its compute power is sitting idle.
How full a delivery truck is when it leaves — 100% utilization means no empty space.

title: VAE
definition: An autoencoder that compresses data into a smooth, organized space you can sample new things from.
examples: Most modern image diffusion models actually run inside a VAE’s compressed space to save compute, not on raw pixels.
Like a librarian who not only files every book but arranges the shelves so similar books sit together — so you can wander to a nearby spot and find something plausible.

title: Validation set
definition: A slice of data the model never trains on, used to tune choices and check progress honestly.
examples: The team compares two learning rates by which one scores better on the validation set, then locks that choice in.
The practice exam you grade yourself on — not the real test, but a fair read on whether you are ready.

title: Value Alignment
definition: Embedding what we care about—fairness, honesty, harm reduction—into the model's behavior.
examples: A hiring model is taught not to discriminate based on gender, even if historical data shows a pattern.
Like teaching a child your family's principles so they know right from wrong when you're not around.

title: Variational Autoencoder
definition: The full name for a VAE — an autoencoder whose middle is a smooth, sampleable space.
examples: When a latent-diffusion image model “decodes” its result to pixels, that decoder is a VAE’s.
A vending machine that not only stores snacks but lays them out so you can dial to a spot between two and get a sensible blend.

title: Vector
definition: A list of numbers that stands in for a thing, so a computer can do math on meaning.
examples: The word “dog” might become [0.2, -1.1, 0.7, …], and “puppy” lands nearby in the same number-space.
GPS coordinates for an idea — a handful of numbers that pin it to a spot you can measure distances from.

title: Vector Index
definition: A data structure that makes finding the nearest vectors fast, even among millions of them.
examples: With ten million embeddings, a vector index returns the closest matches in milliseconds instead of scanning them all.
A library’s shelving system — you don’t walk past every book, the organization takes you near the right shelf instantly.

title: Vector Similarity
definition: The math for how "close" two embeddings are — the thing semantic search actually ranks by.
examples: A search ranks chunks by cosine similarity to the query embedding and returns the top few closest.
Measuring how alike two colors are by how near they sit on the color wheel.

title: Vector database
definition: A database built to store meanings as coordinates and find the nearest ones fast — the memory bank behind RAG.
examples: Ask a support bot a question and it pulls the three closest help-doc chunks from a vector database.
A library shelved by what books are about, not by title — so “nearby” means “similar in meaning.”

title: Versioning
definition: Tracking model changes over time so you can reproduce results, rollback, and understand what changed between versions.
examples: Model v1.0 trained on 2024 data scores 92% accuracy; v1.1 with 2025 data scores 91%—rollback to v1.0 if needed.
Git for your model; each commit is a snapshot with metadata and a message.

title: Vertical scaling
definition: Making a single machine more powerful (more CPU, more GPU, more memory) instead of adding more machines.
examples: Instead of 5 GPU servers, buy 1 with 5 GPUs (or 1 huge GPU).
Buying a bigger truck instead of buying more trucks.

title: Vibe coding
definition: What we briefly called just… talking to an AI until the app worked, without really reading the code.
examples: In 2024, “I vibe-coded a weekend app” meant you prompted your way to something that ran and shipped it.
Cooking without measuring — totally fine for a snack, faintly terrifying for a wedding cake.

title: Video Generation
definition: Generating video sequences with temporal coherence—objects move smoothly, lighting is consistent frame-to-frame.
examples: Model generates a 5-second clip of a sunset over a beach; each frame flows naturally to the next.
A flipbook that the AI draws, frame by frame, with the same consistent characters and environment.

title: Video Understanding
definition: Comprehending what is happening in a video - recognizing actions, events, and relationships across frames.
examples: A video of a person doing yoga: the system identifies the pose, flow, difficulty. A traffic accident video: identifies vehicles, speeds, impact.
Watching a film: you understand the plot, characters, emotions, and story arc, not just individual shots.

title: vision API
definition: An API endpoint that takes an image and returns an analysis—caption, object detection, OCR, reasoning about visual content.
examples: Send a photo of a receipt to Claude's vision API. Get back line items, total, vendor, date—all extracted and structured.
Giving a description of a painting to a blind person; the model translates pixels to words.

title: Vision Model
definition: Neural network trained to process images and understand visual content—classify objects, detect faces, or describe scenes.
examples: ResNet-50 classifies 1000 object categories from ImageNet; YOLO detects people and cars in real-time video.
Teaching a kid to recognize animals in a picture instead of just reading a list of words.

title: Vision Transformer
definition: A transformer architecture applied to images, treating image patches as tokens - enabling pure attention-based vision.
examples: Split a 224x224 image into 16x16 patches (196 patches), embed each, run transformer. Classification: use [CLS] tokens final hidden state.
Like BERT for text, but for images: split image into patches, embed them, apply self-attention.

title: Visual Grounding
definition: Locating which region of an image a text phrase refers to - bridging language and vision.
examples: "The dog wearing a hat" -> system highlights the bounding box or segment of the dog wearing a hat in the image.
Someone says "the red car on the left," and you point to it in the picture.

title: Visual Question Answering
definition: The task of answering natural-language questions about images - combining vision and language understanding.
examples: "What color is the car?" while shown a photo. "How many people are in this room?" over a screenshot. "Is the dog sitting?" - yes or no.
Like a student pointing to a diagram in a textbook and asking "what color is this?" The model sees the image and understands the question.

title: ViT
definition: Shorthand for Vision Transformer - a transformer model for image understanding.
examples: ViT-Base trained on ImageNet; can be fine-tuned on medical imaging, COCO, or used as a backbone for other tasks.
BERT is ViTs sibling: BERT processes text, ViT processes images.

title: vLLM
definition: An inference engine optimized for fast LLM serving — uses PagedAttention to avoid wasteful memory fragmentation.
examples: vLLM can serve more concurrent requests per GPU than vanilla PyTorch because it doesn't allocate a full context window per request upfront.
A smart warehouse manager who packs boxes efficiently so none of the shelf space is wasted.

title: VLM
definition: Neural network that understands both images and text—can caption photos, answer questions about images, or generate images from descriptions.
examples: GPT-4V takes an image and asks "what is in this photo?" and responds "a beach sunset with people swimming"; CLIP retrieves images matching text queries.
A person who can read, write, and understand pictures—richer than someone who only reads or only looks.

title: Vocabulary
definition: The fixed set of tokens a model knows — every piece it can read or write has to come from this list.
examples: A common English word is one token in the vocab; a rare name gets spelled out from several.
The full set of LEGO brick shapes in the box; anything you build uses only those.

title: Vocabulary size
definition: How many distinct tokens the model knows — a trade-off between shorter sequences and a bigger, heavier vocabulary.
examples: Bumping the vocabulary from 32k to 128k tokens lets the model encode the same text in fewer tokens, especially in other languages.
The number of keys on a keyboard: more keys means fewer keystrokes per word, but a bulkier keyboard.

title: Vocoder
definition: A model that converts a spectrogram or other audio representation into a waveform - turning abstract audio features into actual sound.
examples: Text-to-speech pipeline: text -> phonemes -> mel-spectrogram (Tacotron) -> waveform (vocoder like WaveGlow or HiFi-GAN).
A printer for sound: you describe the pattern (spectrogram), and the printer produces the actual sound waves.

title: Voice Cloning
definition: Creating a synthetic voice that sounds like a specific person from a few audio samples—read text in your voice.
examples: 30 seconds of your voice; AI generates "I will call you later" in your accent, tone, and speaking style.
Recording yourself saying different phonemes then auto-combining them to say anything.

title: VQA
definition: Shorthand for visual question answering - the ability to answer questions posed in natural language about visual content.
examples: A VQA system shown a photo with people, trees, and a bench answers "Are there more people or trees?" or "What is the bench made of?"
Like the parlor game "I spy" - someone describes what they see, you guess what it is. VQA is the reverse: you see the image, you answer the description.

title: VRAM
definition: The memory on a GPU, where model weights, activations, and intermediate results live during computation.
examples: A 7B model in BF16 needs 14GB VRAM. Batch size 32 and intermediate computations might need another 20GB. Total: 34GB VRAM.
The scratch pad a calculator uses to store partial results.

title: Warm start
definition: Beginning training from an existing model’s weights instead of from scratch.
examples: Rather than train a new model from zero, a team warm-starts from an open-weights checkpoint and fine-tunes on their data.
Like starting a novel from a detailed outline rather than a blank page.

title: Warmup
definition: Starting training with a small learning rate and ramping it up over the first steps.
examples: For the first 500 steps the learning rate climbs from near zero to its target, so early updates don’t blow up the model.
Like stretching before a sprint — ease in so you don’t pull something at full speed from a cold start.

title: Watermarking
definition: Embedding a hidden, detectable signal in AI output so it can later be identified as machine-made.
examples: A text generator subtly biases its word choices in a statistically detectable pattern, so a checking tool can later flag the passage as likely AI-written.
The faint watermark in a banknote — invisible in normal use, but proof of origin when you hold it to the light.

title: Weak Supervision
definition: Label a mountain of data cheaply with rough rules instead of paying humans to do it all by hand.
examples: To flag toxic comments, you write a few keyword rules and treat their output as labels, then train on millions of examples.
Sorting mail by zip-code stamps instead of reading every envelope — fast, mostly right, occasionally wrong.

title: Weak-to-strong generalization
definition: Whether a weaker teacher can steer a much stronger student to be even better than the teacher itself.
examples: Researchers fine-tune a large model using labels from a smaller, weaker model and find it generalizes past the weak labels’ mistakes.
A grade-school coach who somehow trains an athlete that ends up outperforming anything the coach could ever do.

title: Weaviate
definition: Open-source vector database, self-hosted or managed cloud; for storing and retrieving embeddings and structured data.
examples: Deploy Weaviate in Kubernetes; store document embeddings and metadata; query with Hybrid search (semantic + keyword).
Vector DB you can self-host; more control, more ops work.

title: Web crawl
definition: Text scraped in bulk from across the public internet — the messy backbone of most pretraining data.
examples: A team starts from a raw web crawl of billions of pages, then filters it down to the fraction worth training on.
Emptying the whole internet into a bin and then sorting it — most of the volume, most of the mess.

title: Weight Averaging
definition: Take the numerical average of a model’s weights across runs or checkpoints to get a steadier model.
examples: Instead of shipping the final training step, a team averages the last ten checkpoints and ships that smoother version.
Averaging several thermometer readings to smooth out the jitter in any single one.

title: Weight decay
definition: Gently shrinking weights toward zero during training so the model stays simple and generalizes.
examples: Adding weight decay stops a model from letting a few weights grow huge to memorize training quirks.
Like a tidy-desk rule that quietly clears clutter each day, keeping only what earns its place.

title: Weights
definition: The individual learned numbers inside a model — “the weights” is shorthand for the whole trained brain you can download.
examples: “Open weights” means you can download the numbers and run the model yourself.
The recipe card after all the tweaking — hand someone the weights and they can cook the same dish.

title: Weights and biases
definition: The two kinds of knobs a network learns: weights scale each input, biases nudge the result.
examples: Training a model means slowly turning billions of these weights and biases until the outputs stop being wrong.
A recipe where weights are how much of each ingredient and the bias is the pinch of salt added no matter what.

title: Whisper
definition: OpenAI's open-source speech-to-text model, trained on 680k hours of multilingual audio data.
examples: Transcribe a podcast or meeting recording; handles accents, background noise, and multiple languages.
The boring superpower; speech recognition that just works, in many languages.

title: Win Rate
definition: In pairwise comparisons, the percentage of times judges prefer one model over another—intuitive and human-aligned.
examples: LLM judges compare 100 outputs from Model A and Model B. Model A wins 65 comparisons. Win rate for Model A is 65%.
Like head-to-head match results in a tournament: Model A won 70% of matches against Model B.

title: Word embedding
definition: A word turned into a list of numbers so that similar words land near each other in space.
examples: A classic model places “king” and “queen” close together, and the gap from “man” to “woman” mirrors the gap from “king” to “queen.”
Like giving every word a home address in a city where synonyms are neighbors and opposites live across town.

title: Worker Agent
definition: A focused agent that does one assigned piece of a larger job and reports back.
examples: A worker agent is told only “summarize these five sources,” with no view of the wider project, and returns a tidy summary.
A specialist contractor called in for the wiring — does that one part well, then hands it back to the general contractor.

title: Workflow Engine
definition: A system that runs a defined sequence of steps reliably, handling ordering, retries, and failures.
examples: A workflow engine runs “extract → validate → summarize → email” for every uploaded document, retrying any step that fails.
An assembly line — each station does its part in order, and if one jams, the line knows how to respond.

title: Working Memory
definition: The small, fast scratch space an agent uses to hold what it’s thinking about right now.
examples: While booking a trip, the agent keeps the current dates, budget, and shortlisted flights in working memory, not in long-term storage.
The sticky notes on your desk during a task — grabbed, glanced at, and tossed when you’re done.

title: World model
definition: An internal picture of how things work that lets a system predict what happens next.
examples: A model that tracks who’s holding what across a story — and correctly says the key is now in Sara’s pocket — is showing a small world model.
Like the mental map you use to guess a rolling ball will fall off the table before it does.

title: xAI
definition: Elon Musk's AI company, founded 2023, aiming to build advanced AI systems with a focus on truth-seeking.
examples: Grok (xAI's LLM) released in beta late 2023, integrated with X (Twitter) for real-time information.
The ambitious newcomer: well-funded, claim-driven, building fast.

title: Zero-shot
definition: Asking a model to do a task with no examples at all — just the instruction.
examples: “Classify this review as positive or negative: …” with no sample classifications — the model just does it.
Like handing a capable new hire a task described in one sentence and trusting them to figure it out.

title: Zero-Shot Classification
definition: Classifying images into categories the model has never seen during training - by reasoning about semantic relationships.
examples: CLIP is trained on image-caption pairs. You ask it to classify a photo as one of ["cat", "dog", "elephant"] without ever seeing those three labels in training. It maps the image to embeddings and compares to the class name embeddings.
You know what a "dog" is and what "four-legged" means. Someone shows you a "dachshund" - youve never seen that breed, but you know its a four-legged dog.

title: Zero-shot prompting
definition: Giving a model a task with only instructions, no examples, and expecting it to figure it out on the first try.
examples: You ask a language model "Translate this to French:" and paste text, without showing it any translation examples first.
Asking a smart stranger for directions to a place they've never been: they reason it out from first principles.
